extracted.intended_audience: learned Christians, theologians, and philosophers interested in apologetic arguments for the possibility of bodily resurrection
extracted.subtask_description: A reasoned, natural-philosophy style defence of the possibility of the resurrection of the same bodily person, answering a catalogue of sceptical objections by appeal to Scripture, divine power, and empirical/chemical analogies and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural authority and the Power of God as decisive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: “Do err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the Power of God” (Matt. xxii. v. 29) — the Word you admit to be Divine declares it, and the Power of God is sufficient to perform what He has said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary defence: cite Scripture and remind objectors that God’s omnipotence renders natural improbabilities irrelevant; use Scripture-answer (our Lord's reply to the Sadducees) as the strongest rebuttal to denials of resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is not a greater miracle to raise a body than to create it
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not a greater Miracle to Raise a Body, than to Create it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument strategy: compare the miracle of resurrection with the prior miracle of creation — if creation ex nihilo is accepted, reconstitution from known materials is not intrinsically more incredible. Use this to undercut claims that resurrection is uniquely impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy: human bodies originate from Earth, so resurrection from Earth is plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: All the food of which his Body consists proceeds from the Earth, or is metamorphosed Earth; therefore it is no more strange that his Body, once Earth, should be raised again from the same than that it first acquired its figure from thence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural analogy: because bodies are formed from earth (observed in generation and nourishment), the restoration of a body from earthly particles is a plausible natural correlate of known processes; employ illustrative thought-experiments (man ignorant of food origin) to show the intelligibility of resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument from the common formation of bodies vs. resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: “Even the common Formation of Bodies is less credible than the Resurrection.” — formation from seed/parents appears more mysterious to an ignorant observer than resurrection would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn the sceptic’s standpoint: show that the ordinary process of generation (procreation, embryogenesis) contains puzzles analogous to resurrection; point to empirical facts (e.g., fetal life without respiration) to show that apparent contradictions with experience do not prove impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: That we have no Parents in the Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection that because our first birth requires parents and many natural means, a second birth (resurrection) without parents seems incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reply: God may use different means; point to diversity of reproductive and generative methods in nature (plants/animals) to show the Creator uses many methods; no necessity that same instrumental causes recur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Smallness of the parts after corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection that, after corruption, the body is dissolved into so many small particles that it seems incredible they can be all replaced and ordered to restore the proper body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reply by analogy to human workmanship (anatomist assembling bones, clockmaker reassembling wheels) and optical/dioptric examples (image formed in a dark chamber) to show that widely dispersed particles can obey laws to produce ordered forms; cite experiments showing divine governance of smallest particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Attrition of particles (wear by motion) makes original particles gone
rubrics_metrics.description: Some philosophers argue that the smallest particles wear away with motion, change figure and properties, so that after ages one cannot find the same parts to recombine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter with chemical and preservative examples: many substances persist through repeated unions/changes (nitrous spirit/saltpetre, quicksilver, gold) and embalming or natural cold preserve bodies unchanged for years; conclude attrition does not imply loss of identity of particles or impossibility of preservation/reassembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Union of particles with other bodies — necessity of separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Particles from a putrefied body become united or changed into other bodies (water, air, plants), so reassembly requires not only union but separation from those subsequent bodies — considered highly improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerous chymical examples showing that bodies that unite can be separated again (e.g., dissolving silver in aqua fortis then precipitating it by copper, separation of gold/silver mixtures by aqua fortis, effects of acids/alkalies); show such separations are common in chemistry, so separation at resurrection need not be impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Parts lack uniting properties (we do not observe properties that will make them reunite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replyers claim we cannot observe in parts of human bodies the uniting properties that would bring them together again, therefore resurrection is improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by chemical analogies that union can be effected by adding a third substance or changing conditions (oil+water unites with addition of lye; copper dissolved under certain salts becomes soluble; resins join under some agents), so absence of observed spontaneous uniting properties is not decisive; controlled interventions and differing conditions can enable unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Particles are scattered too far apart for reunion
rubrics_metrics.description: Particles of a body may be dispersed over great distances through ages; bringing them near enough to reunite seems impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter with examples of long-range attractions (amber attracting straw, loadstone drawing iron, gravity acting at astronomical distances); argue that known forces act at great distances and that a greater power can bring widely scattered particles into relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Particles would need to act with choice or knowledge to assemble correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection that among so many millions of particles they would have to 'choose' or act with judgment to reassemble into the correct parts of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide natural analogues: selective affinities in mixtures (loadstone attracts iron alone, quicksilver unites to lead) show differential behavior without conscious choice; menstrua and selective attractions demonstrate that directed assembly can occur by laws of nature rather than volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection: Cannibals — parts consumed by others produce identity confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If one man eats another, the eaten person's parts become part of the cannibal; how can each rise with his own body?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two responses: (1) in many cases nourishment is separated from the body before death, so parts do not remain bound; (2) divine will can prevent particles belonging essentially to two bodies; also chemical examples show addition of a third or change of condition can prevent unions. Emphasize that alimentation and incorporation are governed by God’s will and laws, not necessarily permanent ownership of particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological principle: use of empirical/chemical experiments and analogies to answer metaphysical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: The author repeatedly appeals to experiments and chymical phenomena (preservation in spirits, separation by aqua fortis, precipitation by metals, crystallization of saltpeter, attraction phenomena) to show that natural appearances do not preclude resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive method: marshal concrete experimental instances from chemistry, natural philosophy, anatomy, optics, and geography (preserved frozen bodies) to show analogues to each sceptical difficulty; insist that empirical plausibility of necessary steps suffices even if underlying ultimate principles remain debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of objections into three kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections are classed (Sect. XIII) as (1) unadmissible consequences drawn from accepting resurrection, (2) suppositions of possible things which nevertheless allegedly render resurrection impossible, and (3) apparent contradictions within Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic rubric for rebuttal: treat objections by kind — show alleged consequences are not truly absurd (casework on child/amputee/attenuated bodies), show suppositions fail by empirical counterexample, and reconcile or interpret scriptural texts to remove apparent contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection (example of first kind): absurd consequences about age/limb/size at resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: Three specific 'absurd' consequences: (1) a child dying soon after birth would rise again as a child (imperfect body); (2) someone who loses a limb would rise maimed or disproportional if that limb is not restored; (3) many die wasted or emaciated, so will rise much smaller or imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond by showing divine capacity to provide appropriate restoration, pointing to natural variety in generation and growth, and by arguing that natural processes and divine will can supply proportionate or perfected restoration; treat these as specimens of the class of 'unadmissible consequences' to be handled by appeal to God's methods and to natural analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic claim: It is sufficient to show empirical possibility; one need not resolve deeper natural principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is sufficient to our Purpose if the Experiments be only true, let People deduce them from such Causes, as they shall judge most consistent with their own Hypothesis.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic standard: for the defence of resurrection, demonstrable empirical phenomena that provide analogues or counterexamples suffice; one does not need a complete metaphysical account of the underlying principles to show possibility. Use observed experiments as sufficient warrants.
